topics: ✂️ Thirty-Six Karet Violations — the opening mishna's full list, from forbidden relations to eating chametz on Pesach
🔢 Why Give a Tally? — Rabbi Yoḥanan: one who transgresses all thirty-six in a single lapse brings thirty-six sin offerings
📋 A Gallery of Tallies — the Gemara surveys parallel numbered lists across the Mishna and what each number excludes
👭 Why Single Out One's Sister? — Rabbi Yoḥanan vs. Rav Beivai bar Abaye on Leviticus 20:17
⚖️ Rabbi Yitzḥak's Alternative — karet for one's sister teaches karet overrides lashes, not separation of liability

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Opening the Gate to Karet
overview.subtitle: Keritot 2a–2b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Masechet Keritot opens with its own mishna listing thirty-six transgressions for which the Torah prescribes karet (excision) for intentional violation and a sin offering for unwitting violation. The list spans forbidden sexual relations, blasphemy, idolatry, Molekh, sorcery, Shabbat desecration, impurity in sacred contexts, forbidden fats and blood, notar and piggul, slaughtering offerings outside the Temple, chametz on Pesach, transgressions of Yom Kippur, compounding the anointing oil or incense, and the positive mitzvot of the Paschal offering and circumcision. The Gemara immediately asks why the mishna bothers to state the number thirty-six at all, and Rabbi Yoḥanan answers that the tally teaches a halakha: one who unwittingly violates all thirty-six in a single lapse of awareness is liable to bring a separate sin offering for each. The Gemara then surveys a whole series of other numbered mishnayot to show that tallies always teach something, before turning to why karet for intercourse with one's sister is singled out in its own verse.

slides.title: ✂️ The Mishna's Thirty-Six
slides.subtitle: Every case in the Torah punishable by karet for intentional violation
rows: Mother, father's wife, daughter-in-law, male intercourse, bestiality, woman and her daughter, married woman, sister, father's/mother's/wife's sister, brother's wife, niddah
Blasphemy, idol worship, giving offspring to Molekh, necromancy, desecrating Shabbat
Impure person eating sacrificial food, impure person entering the Temple, eating forbidden fat, blood, notar, piggul, slaughtering and offering outside the Temple
Eating chametz on Pesach, eating or working on Yom Kippur, blending the anointing oil or incense, applying the anointing oil
Failing to bring the Paschal offering; failing to circumcise

callout.label: The pattern:
callout.text: For each of these: intentional violation brings karet; unwitting violation brings a sin offering; and uncertainty brings a provisional guilt offering (asham talui) — except for one who defiles the Temple, says Rabbi Meir, since that case already carries a sliding-scale offering.

slides.title: 🔢 Why State the Number at All?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara's opening question on the mishna

nodes.content: ❓ Why does the mishna say 'thirty-six'? One could simply count the list!
💡 Rabbi Yoḥanan: the tally teaches that if one performed all thirty-six in one lapse of awareness, he is liable for each separately
📜 Proof text: 'For whoever shall do any of these abominations...shall be cut off' (Leviticus 18:29) — teaches liability, not exemption

columns.label: Possible reading
columns.content: One who transgresses all thirty-six together is liable for only one sin offering, like transgressing once

columns.label: Actual halakha
columns.content: He brings thirty-six separate sin offerings — one for each prohibition

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: The number in the mishna is not decorative — it fixes how many separate offerings a person owes.

slides.title: 📋 Tallies Elsewhere in the Mishna
slides.subtitle: The Gemara shows every numbered list in the Mishna excludes a dissenting opinion

boxes.title: Excluding a larger count
items: 39 primary labors (Shabbat 73a) — teaches liability for each if done in one lapse
4 mechusrei kappara — excludes Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov's 'five' (adding a convert)
4 primary categories of damage (Bava Kamma 2a) — excludes Rabbi Oshaya's 13, Rabbi Ḥiyya's 24

boxes.title: Excluding a smaller count
items: 4 who bring an offering for intentional as for unwitting sin — excludes Rabbi Shimon, who removes the false oath on a deposit
5 who bring one offering for many transgressions — needed for the nazirite clause

boxes.title: Setting up a later clause
items: 5 who bring one offering for many transgressions — sets up the case of a nazirite impure on the seventh day twice, per Rabbi Yosei bei Rabbi Yehuda
5 who bring a sliding-scale offering — excludes Rabbi Eliezer, who has the king bring a goat instead

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: Every time the Mishna states a number, the Gemara assumes it comes to exclude some other tanna's count — never mere description.

slides.title: 👭 Why Is Karet for One's Sister Singled Out?
slides.subtitle: Leviticus 20:17 states karet for a sister separately from the general verse — why?

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Granted one is not entirely exempt for violating all forbidden relations together — Leviticus 18:29 says 'whoever does any of these abominations...shall be cut off'. But why not say: one transgression, one offering; all of them together in one lapse, still only one offering?

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: That is why karet for one's sister was singled out (Leviticus 20:17) — to separate the prohibitions, teaching a distinct liability for each forbidden relation.

lines.speaker: Rav Beivai
lines.text: Objects: say instead that only intercourse with a sister — explicitly detailed — earns its own offering, while all the other relations done together in one lapse still yield only one!

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: But doesn't Rav Beivai accept the hermeneutical rule that something singled out from a generalization teaches its halakha for the whole generalization — as with peace offerings among consecrated foods?

lines.speaker: Rav Beivai
lines.text: That rule applies only to cases similar to what was singled out. A sister is unique: forbidden forever, with no possible permission in her brother's lifetime — unlike a married woman, whom divorce can permit.

callout.label: Resolution:
callout.text: Rabbi Yona (or Rav Huna b. Rav Yehoshua) answers from the juxtaposition in Leviticus 18:29 itself: all forbidden relations are equated to the sister for separate liability, even without full similarity.

slides.title: ⚖️ Rabbi Yitzḥak's Different Reading
slides.subtitle: A dissenting tanna reassigns the purpose of the sister-verse entirely

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Yitzḥak: all cases of forbidden relations were already included in the general karet verse (Lev. 18:29) — nothing new there
2️⃣ So why single out karet for a sister (Lev. 20:17)? Not to separate liability, but to establish that she is judged by karet, not lashes

3️⃣ Separation of liability, for Rabbi Yitzḥak, instead comes from a different verse: 'a woman...as long as she is impure by her menstruation' (Lev. 18:19) — its extra words teach a separate penalty for each woman

4️⃣ Then what does 'his sister' at the verse's end (Lev. 20:17) add? It teaches separate liability for a woman who is simultaneously one's sister, father's sister, and mother's sister — three offerings for one act

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: Two tannaim reach the same practical halakha of separate liability for each forbidden relation, but derive it from two different verses with two different roles for the sister-verse.

summary.principle: The mishna's tally of thirty-six karet violations is not incidental; it teaches that one who transgresses them all in a single lapse of awareness is liable to bring a separate sin offering for each.

flowSteps.content: ✂️ Mishna: 36 transgressions carry karet for intentional violation, a sin offering for unwitting violation
❓ Why state the number 36 at all?
🔢 R' Yoḥanan: to teach liability for each violation separately, even if all done in one lapse

columns.content: 📋 Every numbered mishna in Shas works the same way — excluding some other count
👭 Sister singled out in Lev. 20:17 — R' Yoḥanan: to separate liability; R' Yitzḥak: to fix the penalty as karet

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a stated tally in the Mishna always excludes a rival opinion, never mere counting

quiz.q: According to the opening mishna, how many transgressions in the Torah carry a punishment of karet for intentional violation?
o: Twenty-four
Thirty-nine
Thirty-six
Forty
quiz.e: The mishna opens by listing thirty-six categories of transgression punishable by karet.

quiz.q: Why, according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, does the mishna state the number 'thirty-six' instead of simply listing the cases?
o: To help students memorize the list
To teach that one who transgresses all of them in a single lapse of awareness is liable for each one separately
To exclude a case not really punishable by karet
To indicate the order in which they occurred at Sinai
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that the tally teaches that one who violates all thirty-six unwittingly in one lapse of awareness must bring thirty-six separate sin offerings.

quiz.q: What halakha does Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov's dissenting view about 'five' mechusrei kappara (rather than four) add?
o: That the leper needs two offerings
That a convert is also considered lacking atonement until the blood of his offering is sprinkled
That the zav is exempt from an offering
That the woman after childbirth is like a zava
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov holds a convert is a fifth person who lacks atonement, needing the sprinkling of his offering's blood before eating consecrated food; the mishna's 'four' excludes this view.

quiz.q: Why, according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, is karet for intercourse with one's sister mentioned in its own separate verse (Leviticus 20:17)?
o: To teach that this transgression alone bears karet
To exempt it from a sin offering
To separate this and all other forbidden relations, teaching a distinct liability for each one
To teach that only lashes apply, not karet
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the singling-out of the sister teaches that every forbidden relation generates a separate liability rather than all being punished as one.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yitzḥak understand the purpose of singling out karet for one's sister in Leviticus 20:17?
o: To teach that she alone carries karet while all others carry only lashes
To teach that she is judged by karet rather than lashes, since forbidden relations were already generally included under karet
To exempt an unwitting sinner entirely
To teach that a sister requires two sin offerings
quiz.e: Rabbi Yitzḥak holds that all forbidden relations were already covered by the general karet verse (Lev. 18:29); the sister-verse instead establishes that her punishment is specifically karet rather than lashes.
